question: When you click to park a distance number, which part of the number should land on your click?
context: Measuring a distance takes three clicks and the last one parks the number. Your click becomes the middle of the number, so clicking into the 24 points of gap under a button leaves the number touching the button. This decides what that last click should mean.

options.label: Leave it: your click is the middle
options.summary: Nothing changes. The number centres on the spot you click, so half of it grows back toward the thing you just measured. Click into a gap that is narrower than the number is tall and it ends up touching what you measured.
pros: Nothing moves for anyone already used to it
The number is always exactly centred on the spot you pointed at
There is no second rule to learn
cons: Clicking into a narrow gap leaves the number hard against the thing you measured
To get any air you have to aim half a number's height clear of the edge, which is not a thing anyone can judge by eye
options.mitigation: The number is now drawn under your pointer while you aim, so the crowding is at least visible before you commit rather than after.

options.label: Your click is the near edge
options.summary: The number grows away from what you measured instead of straddling your click. Click 24 points under a button and the top of the number lands on that spot, with the rest of it below.
pros: A click anywhere just off an element leaves clean air between the two
The gap you point into is the gap you get
It works the same whichever side of the measurement you park on
cons: The number always ends about half its own height further out than the exact spot you clicked
Parking it out in open space, where nothing was in the way, it still sits a little past where you pointed
options.mitigation: The number rides under your pointer while you aim, so the offset is on screen the whole time instead of arriving on the click.

options.label: Your click is the middle, but it never crowds what you measured
options.summary: The number still centres on your click. The one time it moves is when it would land right up against the thing you just measured: then it slides out far enough to leave a hair of air, the same air the Size and Gap numbers already keep.
pros: A click in open space puts the number exactly where you pointed
The only case that changes is the one case that reads badly, a number touching the element
It is the same standoff Size and Gap already keep, so all three ways of measuring look alike
cons: The click means two slightly different things depending on what is nearby
It can only stand clear of something it can see in the picture, so a measurement across empty space has nothing to keep off
options.mitigation: The number rides under your pointer while you aim, so on the occasions it does slide you see where it will sit before you commit.
